**The Old Night**

If you could stand in the English countryside in the year 1600, past midnight, you would not be able to see your own hands. This is hard to picture now, and the difficulty itself is worth examining. We think we know what darkness is: the room with the lights off, the street at 3 a.m. with its orange pools and hard shadows. But that is twilight compared to what darkness used to be. On a moonless night, the world simply vanished. The path disappeared. Travelers hired guides not because roads were complicated but because the road was literally not there—only a memory of it under their boots and the sound of it somewhere ahead.

People organized their lives around what light existed. The moon was not romantic scenery; it was infrastructure. Harvests were brought in by full-moon light—the harvest moon was a work schedule before it was a poem. And the stars—honestly, the stars. Every human being who ever lived before the modern era saw the Milky Way on a clear night, saw it so plainly that cultures all over the planet independently named it a river, a road, a spine of heaven. Sailors steered by it. Cosmologies were built from what was visible to anyone who simply looked up.

One of the strangest facts from this lost world is that people slept differently. The historian Roger Ekirch, combing through diaries, court records, and medical texts spanning centuries, found the same phrase recurring in dozens of languages: "first sleep" and "second sleep." People went to bed not long after dark, slept a few hours, then woke for an hour or two in the middle of the night—and this was so ordinary that no one thought to explain it. They prayed. They talked. They visited neighbors by moonlight. They made love, they smoked, they lay thinking about dreams which, uninterrupted by screens and electric noise, apparently arrived thick and vivid in that drowsy interval. Then they sank back into the second sleep until dawn. Decades later, sleep researchers deprived volunteers of electric light and watched them spontaneously revert to exactly this pattern. The implication is quietly astonishing: segmented sleep may be the human default. Given real darkness, our bodies remember something we have forgotten.

Then we killed the night. Not all at once—first candles, then oil, then the gas lamps of the early 1800s, which cities adopted with civic pride, and finally electricity, which was not a lamp added to the darkness but a decision that darkness would end. Night became a dim, inconvenient version of day. And because night was now merely dim rather than dangerous, it became useful. Factories discovered they could run around the clock. Today the takeover is complete: satellite photographs of Earth at night show the continents laced with light, the great cities glowing like infections on a chart.

We gained enormously, and it's worth saying so plainly. Night is where I am writing this, and probably where you are reading it. Nobody romanticizes stumbling into a ditch, or the old and reasonable fear of the road after dark. But honesty requires naming what we traded away. Roughly eighty percent of North Americans, and a third of all humanity, can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. Most people now live and die without once seeing, with their own eyes, the galaxy they live inside. And the loss is not only aesthetic. Excess light at night suppresses melatonin and scrambles our circadian timing. It disorients billions of migrating birds, pulls insects away from the plants that need them, and lures sea-turtle hatchlings away from the sea and toward the glow of beachfront hotels.

The deeper loss is harder to measure. Night used to be a different country, and we are the first generations never to have emigrated there. We experience darkness as an absence—a gap in the schedule, a condition to be fixed with a phone screen. We don't have midnight hours of our own anymore; we just have the day, extended. The old rhythm is so alien to us that when we wake at 3 a.m., we no longer think, *first sleep has ended*; we think something is wrong with us. We lie there anxious, or reach for the phone—the very instrument of the light that abolished the interval in the first place.

I wonder sometimes if there's a homesickness in us for a place we've never been. It seems telling that when people want to describe awe, they still reach for the stars—stars most of them have never actually seen. There is now a small industry of dark-sky preserves, where the last darkness is kept in fenced reserves like an endangered species, and people drive for hours to stand in a field while a guide with a laser pointer shows them the Milky Way, the way you'd be shown a rare bird. What those people report, almost always, is not beauty exactly, or not only beauty. It's a kind of vertigo. A recalibration of scale.

Every once in a while, run the experiment yourself. Drive out past the last town, past where the orange domes of the suburbs stop flattening the horizon, and stop on some back road, and kill the lights. Give your eyes their full half hour—the pupils opening all the way, the retina slowly manufacturing the chemistry of night vision that we almost never allow to finish its work. Then look up. That is the view every ancestor you ever had considered ordinary. It was the ceiling of every story ever told around a fire. We are, as far as we know, the first people to lose it, and we lost it in four generations—less than a single long human lifespan.

Which means there are babies being born tonight who could see it again, if we decided the night was worth keeping dark in at least a few places. Not because darkness is useful. Because we are creatures who were shaped by the old night, and it seems a strange mercy to let someone live their whole life without ever learning what shaped them.
